text: (i)1 Describe the main way carbon dioxide is transported in the blood.
say: For part one 1, describe it: say what happens, step by step. That's one point, for three marks.

text: Plasma: the liquid that carries almost everything.
say: Just over half of your blood is plasma, a watery liquid. It carries dissolved food, hormones, urea, carbon dioxide and heat around the body.

text: White blood cells: fight infection.
say: White blood cells have a nucleus and fight infection. Phagocytes, like monocytes, swallow germs, and lymphocytes make antibodies.

text: Platelets: help blood to clot.
say: Platelets are tiny pieces of cells. At a cut, they help the blood to clot, which stops the bleeding and keeps germs out.

text: Red blood cells: built to carry oxygen
say: Red blood cells: built to carry oxygen

text: (i)2 Describe the main way oxygen is transported in the blood.
say: For part one 2, describe it: say what happens, step by step. That's one point, for three marks.

text: Haemoglobin: with iron, picks up oxygen.
say: They're packed with haemoglobin, a protein containing iron. It picks up oxygen in the lungs and lets it go in the tissues. Most carbon dioxide travels back in the plasma.

text: No nucleus: more room, but a short life.
say: A mature red blood cell has no nucleus, which leaves more room for haemoglobin. But it can't divide or repair itself, so it only lives about 120 days. New ones are made in the bone marrow.

text: Biconcave and flexible: a big surface for gases.
say: Their biconcave shape gives a large surface for oxygen to pass through, and they're flexible enough to squeeze through the narrowest capillaries.

text: Two circuits: the double circulation
say: Two circuits: the double circulation

text: Pulmonary circuit: right side to the lungs and back.
say: The right ventricle pumps blood along the pulmonary artery to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen. It comes back in the pulmonary vein to the left atrium.

text: Systemic circuit: left side to the body and back.
say: The left ventricle pumps that oxygenated blood into the aorta and out to the whole body, at a much higher pressure. It returns, low in oxygen, through the vena cava.

text: Named vessels: renal, hepatic, coronary.
say: Each organ has its own vessels, like the renal artery and vein for the kidneys. Arteries always carry blood away from the heart, and veins always bring it back.

text: Blood groups
say: Blood groups

text: ABO: antigens A, B, both or neither.
say: In the ABO system, your red cells carry antigen A, antigen B, both, or neither. That makes you group A, B, AB or O.

text: Antibodies: against the ones you don't have.
say: Your plasma has antibodies against the antigens you don't have. Give someone the wrong group, and their antibodies make the donated cells clump together.

text: Rhesus: positive or negative.
say: The Rhesus system is a second marker. It matters in pregnancy, when a Rhesus negative mother carries a Rhesus positive baby.

say: For part two, describe it: say what happens, step by step. That's one point, for three marks.

text: Four chambers: two atria on top, two ventricles below.
say: Blood comes into the two atria at the top, then drops into the two ventricles below, which do the hard pumping.

text: The septum: keeps the two sides apart.
say: A wall of muscle called the septum keeps the two sides apart, so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood never mix. The left ventricle has the thickest wall, because it pumps blood all the way round the body.

text: Valves: keep blood going one way.
say: The tricuspid and bicuspid valves stop blood flowing back into the atria, and the semilunar valves stop it flowing back from the arteries. The valves snapping shut make the lub-dub sound of your heartbeat.

say: The pacemaker: the heart's own rhythm

text: SA node: the pacemaker, in the right atrium.
say: In the wall of the right atrium there's a small patch of cells called the SA node: the pacemaker. It sends out an electrical impulse, and the atria contract.

text: AV node: passes it on to the ventricles.
say: The AV node, low in the septum, picks up the impulse and passes it down to the ventricles, so they contract just after the atria.

text: Systole and diastole: contracting, then relaxing.
say: When heart muscle contracts, that's systole. When it relaxes and fills up again, that's diastole. Heart muscle never tires, and it's packed with mitochondria for the energy it needs.

text: (v) In the space below, model one structural difference between an artery and a vein, by describing the difference and/or by drawing a labelled diagram.

text: Arteries: thick, elastic, high pressure.
say: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Their walls are thick, with muscle and elastic fibres to take the high pressure, and their lumen is narrow.

text: Veins: thin walls, wide lumen, valves.
say: Veins bring blood back to the heart at low pressure. They have thin walls, a wide lumen and valves, and the squeeze of the muscles around them keeps the blood moving.

text: Capillaries: one cell thick: for exchange.
say: Capillaries link the two. Their walls are just one cell thick, so oxygen, food and waste pass easily between the blood and the cells.

text: The heart's own blood supply
say: The heart's own blood supply

text: Coronary arteries: branch off the aorta.
say: The coronary arteries branch off the aorta, right at its base, and spread over the surface of the heart, bringing oxygen and food to the heart muscle.

text: A blockage: fat, then a clot.
say: Fatty deposits of cholesterol can build up inside a coronary artery and narrow it. A blood clot can then block it completely.

text: Heart attack: muscle without oxygen dies.
say: The heart muscle beyond the block gets no oxygen, can't respire, and dies. That's a heart attack. Not smoking, a healthy diet and regular exercise all lower the risk.

text: Pulse and blood pressure
say: Pulse and blood pressure

text: Pulse: an artery stretching with each beat.
say: Your pulse is an artery stretching and relaxing each time the left ventricle pumps. You can feel it where an artery runs close to the surface, like your wrist or your neck.

text: Blood pressure: the push on the vessel walls.
say: Blood pressure is the force the blood puts on the walls of the blood vessels. It's highest in the arteries, and it falls as the blood moves on through the capillaries into the veins.

text: Exercise: a faster rate, then recovery.
say: When you exercise, your heart rate rises to bring more oxygen to your muscles and carry away carbon dioxide. A fitter person's rate rises less, and recovers faster.

text: The general defence system
say: The general defence system

text: Barriers: skin, mucus, acid.
say: Your skin is a tough barrier. Mucus traps microbes, cilia sweep them away, and acid in your stomach kills most of what you swallow.

text: Phagocytes: engulf and digest.
say: Any pathogen that gets through meets the phagocytes, like monocytes and macrophages. They engulf it, and digest it with enzymes.

text: Not specific: the same for every invader.
say: These defences treat every invader the same way, and they're always ready. That's why this is called the general, or innate, system.

text: Testing a new vaccine
say: Testing a new vaccine

text: (i) Why was it important to test the vaccine on people from all over the world?
say: For part one, explain it: say what happens, and why. That's one point, for three marks.

text: A control group: gets a placebo.
say: Half the volunteers get the vaccine. The other half, the control group, get a placebo: a harmless injection with no vaccine in it, so the two groups can be compared fairly.

text: A big sample: from everywhere.
say: Tens of thousands of people, from many countries, take part. A large, varied sample makes the results more reliable, and true for everyone.

text: Only who was tested: no further than the data.
say: And the conclusion can only cover the people who were tested. If no children took part, we can't say it works for children.

text: Pathogens: what makes us ill
say: Pathogens: what makes us ill

text: Many kinds: bacteria, viruses, fungi and more.
say: Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists like the one that causes malaria, and even parasitic worms.

text: Prions: misfolded proteins.
say: The oddest are prions: proteins folded into the wrong shape. They cause brain diseases like BSE and CJD, with no cells and no genes at all.

text: Foreign markers: antigens give them away.
say: Every pathogen carries molecules on its surface that your body doesn't recognise. These antigens are how your immune system knows something is wrong.

text: How diseases spread
say: How diseases spread

text: Getting about: travel, touch, water, mosquitoes.
say: Pathogens spread through the air, through touch, food and water, or carried by animals like mosquitoes, and travel takes them around the world.

text: No immunity: and it spreads fast.
say: In a population with no immunity, like the rabbits hit by myxomatosis, or people who haven't been vaccinated, a disease can spread very quickly.

text: Immunity builds: and the death rate falls.
say: Over time the survivors, and their offspring, can be immune, so the disease kills fewer of them.

text: What is a virus?
say: What is a virus?

text: Two parts: nucleic acid in a protein coat.
say: Every virus has just two main parts: its genes, made of DNA or RNA, packed inside a coat of protein called the capsid.

text: No cells: so is it living?
say: It has no cells, no organelles and no metabolism of its own. That's why biologists find it so hard to call a virus living.

text: Obligate parasite: it needs a host cell.
say: A virus can only reproduce inside a living host cell. On its own, it simply waits. That makes it an obligate parasite.

say: For part one, read the diagram and find the exact part. That's two points, for three marks.

text: How a virus multiplies
say: How a virus multiplies

text: Attach and enter: its nucleic acid gets in.
say: First, the virus attaches to a host cell, and its DNA or RNA gets inside.

text: Copies: made by the host cell.
say: Then the host cell's own ribosomes, enzymes and energy are used to copy the viral genes and make new protein coats.

text: Assembled and released: the cell often bursts.
say: The parts are assembled into hundreds of new viruses, which burst out of the cell to infect the next one.

text: Harmful and helpful viruses
say: Harmful and helpful viruses

text: Harmful: colds, flu, measles, HIV.
say: Viruses cause the common cold, flu, measles, COVID-19 and AIDS in people, and diseases like tobacco mosaic in plants.

text: Helpful: carrying genes.
say: But scientists can use them to carry useful genes into cells. That's genetic engineering, with the virus as the vector.

text: Bacteriophages: viruses that kill bacteria.
say: Some viruses, called bacteriophages, attack only bacteria. They could be used to treat infections that antibiotics can no longer cure.

say: B and T lymphocytes

text: (i) 1. Lymphocytes, such as the one shown in the diagram, mature in the lymphatic system, which is part of the human defence system. 1. Name two organs of the lymphatic system.

text: B cells: make antibodies.
say: Lymphocytes are made in the bone marrow. B lymphocytes make antibodies against the antigens they recognise.

text: T cells: helper, killer, suppressor, memory.
say: Helper T cells recognise antigens and switch the other lymphocytes on. Killer T cells find infected cells and burst them with a chemical called perforin.

text: Off, and remember: suppressor and memory cells.
say: Suppressor T cells switch the attack off when it's over. Memory cells stay for years, ready for the next time.

text: Vaccination and immunity
say: Vaccination and immunity

text: Harmless dose: a weakened or dead pathogen.
say: A vaccine is a harmless form of a pathogen, weakened, dead, or just its antigens, put into the body.

text: Active immunity: your own antibodies and memory cells.
say: Your body makes its own antibodies and memory cells against it. That's active immunity, and it can last for years.

text: Passive immunity: ready-made antibodies.
say: Passive immunity is when you're given ready-made antibodies, from an injection, or from breast milk. It works straight away, but fades within weeks.

text: Antibiotics and resistance
say: Antibiotics and resistance

text: Antibiotics: made by microbes, kill bacteria.
say: An antibiotic is a substance made by a micro-organism, like penicillin from a fungus, that kills bacteria or stops them growing.

text: Not viruses: no effect on them at all.
say: They have no effect on viruses. So antibiotics won't cure a cold, the flu or COVID-19.

text: Resistance: natural selection at work.
say: When antibiotics are overused, a few bacteria with resistance genes survive and multiply. Soon the whole population is resistant, and the antibiotic stops working.
